content: The cost of preventing one HIV infection (HIA) in adults through voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) ranged from $117 in Kenya (Marseille, 2014) to $4949 in Rwanda (Binagwaho, 2010). For adolescents, the cost per HIA ranged from $804 to $3932 (Binagwaho, 2010; Tumwesigye, 2013). Variability in these estimates is likely due to differences in HIV prevalence rates across African countries and the use of region-specific data within countries, which may limit generalizability. However, some studies, such as those by Bautista-Arredondo (2018), Galárraga (2009), Uthman (2010), and White (2008), provided cost data for larger populations across Africa, offering better generalizability. A systematic review of five VMMC studies in South Africa, Uganda, Lesotho, Swaziland, and sub-Saharan Africa reported the cost per VMMC procedure in South Africa to be $55 (Galárraga, 2009). The cost per HIA for interventions targeting individuals aged 15–49 years over different time periods was as follows: $1806 for 2 years, $974 for 5 years, $431 for 10 years, $195 for 20 years, $132 for 30 years, $104 for 40 years, and $89 for 50 years (White, 2008). In Malawi, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania, and Uganda, the lowest cost per HIA was achieved by circumcising males aged 15–34 years (Kripke, 2016a). A systematic review by Uthman (2010) on adult VMMC for HIV prevention in men demonstrated that VMMC is cost-effective and potentially cost-saving. The cost per HIA in this review ranged from $174 to $2808. Recent data on the average cost per VMMC client from 107 facilities in Kenya, Rwanda, South Africa, and Zambia showed unit costs ranging from $66 in Kenya to $160 in South Africa (Bautista-Arredondo, 2018). Staff costs were the largest component of VMMC unit costs, followed by circumcision kits and HIV test kits. Nurses were the primary providers of VMMC in Rwanda, South Africa, and Zambia, while physicians played a more significant role in Kenya and South Africa. Task-shifting from physicians to clinical officers in Uganda resulted in cost savings, particularly in mobile camps and static centers (Alfonso, 2016). Efficiency gains from guided training for clinicians at the start of program implementation also contributed to cost reductions, with savings of 46–59% reported in Uganda (Kuznik, 2012). Supply-side factors, such as the level of service provision (primary healthcare facilities vs. hospitals), task-shifting, staff experience, and VMMC outreach, were associated with variations in VMMC costs. Improvements in these factors led to cost reductions. No significant limitations in study validity or generalizability were noted for cost estimations. Following the 2007 WHO recommendations for VMMC, evidence from modeling studies and systematic reviews highlighted its cost-effectiveness. VMMC was identified as one of 44 essential surgical procedures by the World Bank Disease Control Priorities Third Edition (Debas, 2015). Studies conducted across various African countries, including Rwanda, South Africa, Uganda, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Tanzania, and Kenya, consistently demonstrated the cost-effectiveness of VMMC. In Tanzania, a demand strategy intervention had a lower cost per HIA compared to standard care, with costs of $1424 vs. $1917 in Njombe and $2212 vs. $3018 in Tabora (Torres-Rueda, 2018). VMMC remained cost-effective even at higher costs, such as $69 per circumcision in Lesotho and Swaziland, with cost-effectiveness estimates of $292 and $176, respectively (Galárraga, 2009). The DMPPT model projected that scaling up circumcision to 80% coverage in five-year age strata from 2014–2018 in Malawi, South Africa, Swaziland, Uganda, and Tanzania would significantly reduce HIV incidence over 15 years. The greatest reductions in annual HIV risk occurred for circumcisions performed around age 25, corresponding to the age of highest HIV incidence. Circumcising younger men (under 30 years) had a greater absolute impact on the number of HIAs and resulted in fewer circumcisions per infection averted and lower costs per infection averted. Adolescent VMMC was found to be highly cost-effective, but this cost-effectiveness was sensitive to small changes in input variables. Adult VMMC was not as cost-saving or highly cost-effective when considering only the direct benefits for the circumcised man (Binagwaho, 2010). In Zimbabwe, circumcising males aged 15–19 contributed the most to HIV incidence reduction, with additional contributions from males aged 20–29 (Kripke, 2016a). In South Africa and Tanzania, the lowest cost per HIA was achieved by circumcising males aged 15–34, while in Malawi and Uganda, focusing on males aged 15–34 or 15–49 was most cost-effective (Kripke, 2016b). Barriers to VMMC implementation included transportation challenges, lack of peer support, limited knowledge about VMMC's protective benefits, fear of pain, and cultural or religious resistance. Facilitators included engaging parents and school personnel, addressing misconceptions, and ensuring affordable or free services. Strategies to improve uptake included implementing interventions after exams, educating communities, and addressing service-related barriers such as long waiting times and staff shortages.
